notes:
These are verse-by-verse notes on 1 Samuel 26. A few gaps first. I ran out of research steps before I could read anything on netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, so there are no Catholic or Orthodox notes. I also found no Protestant traditions disagreeing with each other on this chapter, so that part is not covered either (see the end). Two commentary pages wouldn't load (the Pulpit and Ellicott full chapters), so for those I only have the excerpts that appeared in search results.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- The Ziphites had already told Saul where David was once before (23:19–23). Now they hope to win the king's favour again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- One reason suggested is political calculation: siding with the reigning king looked safer than backing an outlaw. The commentary cites Proverbs 29:25, "The fear of man brings a snare." https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/26.htm
- Background: Gibeah was Saul's hometown, identified with Tell el-Ful, about four miles north of Jerusalem. Hachilah lies in the Wilderness of Ziph, a barren limestone region south of Hebron. https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/26.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: after marrying Abigail, David naturally went back to Maon. The Ziphites were likely to report him because they feared he would take revenge for their earlier betrayal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-26.html

**v. 2**
- Saul is breaking the repentance he showed in 24:16–21. Guzik calls that repentance deep and sincere but short-lived. He also notes the odds: 3,000 men against David's 600. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- Coffman points out that 3,000 was the number of men Saul always kept with him (13:2; 24:2; 26:2). So the same number in chapters 24 and 26 proves nothing about the two stories being one. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/1-samuel-26.html

**vv. 3–4**
- Matthew Henry: David acted defensively. He did not march out to fight, and he sought his own safety, not Saul's ruin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_026.cfm
- Guzik: David sent spies like a capable commander. He knew where Saul was, but Saul did not know where David was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/

**v. 5**
- The KJV's "trench" is accurate to the Hebrew but misleading. The idea is the edge of the camp, marked out by the wagons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- In chapter 24 Saul stumbled onto David by chance. Here David goes looking for Saul, and goes himself rather than sending one of his men, which shows his courage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/

**v. 6**
- Abishai was the son of David's sister Zeruiah, so he was David's nephew. His eagerness to strike looks ahead to his later career as one of David's mightiest warriors. https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/26.htm
- Abishai and Joab later became key leaders of Israel's army under King David. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-spares-saul-again

**v. 7**
- Saul was asleep near Abner, his army commander, with his spear stuck in the ground by his head. He was completely vulnerable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/

**v. 8**
- As in 24:4, David's men treat the moment as God's doing, a chance for righteous revenge. Abishai offers to do it himself, so David could say he had not killed Saul. Guzik also sees "poetic justice" in using the same spear Saul had thrown at David (18:10–11; 19:9–10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- The Hebrew verb for "delivered" (natan) suggests God handing something over. https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/26.htm

**v. 9**
- David's answer to Abishai starts (v. 9) and ends (v. 11) with the same reason: Saul is the LORD's anointed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-26.html
- God anointed Saul, so only God may remove him. "Guiltless" translates a Hebrew word meaning clean or acquitted. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-26-commentary
- David knew Saul was deeply in sin. But even a sinning king stays the anointed king (10:1) until God changes that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh): David is the commander of 600 men. If he lets anyone kill Saul, the guilt is really his. https://bible.org/seriespage/second-time-around-1-samuel-261-25

**v. 10**
- Pett: David lists the three ways a king might expect to die: struck by God, natural death, or death in battle. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/1-samuel-26.html
- Pulpit: David leaves it all to God. But if Saul is to die violently, he should fall with honour in battle against Israel's enemies, not at the hand of his own subject. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-26.html
- Here David goes further than in chapter 24: he states outright that God himself will remove Saul. https://bible.org/seriespage/second-time-around-1-samuel-261-25
- Guzik links this to Romans 12:19, "Vengeance is Mine." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/

**v. 11**
- Constable: David came into the camp to teach Saul a lesson, not to kill him. Taking the spear showed that he had the power of death and chose not to use it. It also hinted that the right to rule would one day be David's. In the wilderness, life depended on water, so the jug made the same point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-26.html
- Ligonier, on the parallel in chapter 24: God never told David to assassinate Saul. Doing so would have meant winning the kingdom by illicit means. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-spares-sauls-life

**v. 12**
- The Cambridge Bible says the Hebrew word for "deep sleep" is used especially of sleep caused by God, as in Genesis 2:21 and 15:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/26-12.htm
- Gill finds it extraordinary that none of 3,000 men woke, not even the sentries. He suggests David may have carried the items himself so that Abishai would not be tempted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/26-12.htm
- Ligonier: David and Abishai could only do something so bold because the LORD had put the army to sleep. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-spares-saul-again
- Matthew Henry's lesson: Saul lost his spear (strength) and his water (comfort) while asleep. So do we when we are careless and off guard. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/26-12.html

**vv. 13–16**
- David crossed a ravine to put distance between himself and Saul. He spoke to Abner because Abner was responsible for leaving the king unguarded. The man who "came to destroy" the king was Abishai. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-26.html
- David, not Saul's bodyguard Abner, is the one who actually saved Saul's life. Abner deserved to die but was spared as well. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-26.html
- Bible.org: Saul is still breathing only because David stopped Abishai. https://bible.org/seriespage/second-time-around-1-samuel-261-25
- Guzik: David implied that he cared more about Saul's life than Abner did. The spear and jug were proof, like the piece of robe in 24:11. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- Bob Roe (quoted on Precept Austin) thinks this humiliation may be a basic reason Abner later kept the ten tribes from joining David. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-26-commentary

**v. 17**
- Constable notes that this time David does not call Saul "father," as he had before. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-26.html
- Guzik: the repeated "my lord… your servant" shows real humility, even though David was in the right. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/

**v. 18**
- David asks Saul to look at the facts: what has he actually done? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- Pett: in chapter 24 David offers his mercy as proof of his innocence. Here he angrily demands to know why Saul is still chasing him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/1-samuel-26.html

**v. 19**
- "Accept an offering" can be read several ways:
  - Benson and JFB: a sacrifice offered by both of them to calm God's anger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/26-19.htm
  - Clarke: let God take David's own life as the sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/26-19.html
  - Gill: a sin offering, a prayer (as the Targum and Jarchi say), or a joint sacrifice for reconciliation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/26-19.html
- Barnes: "the LORD stirred you up" refers to the evil spirit from God that started the persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/26-19.htm
- Cambridge: Hebrew thinking did not separate what God causes from what he permits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/26-19.htm
- JFB admires David's tact in blaming slanderers rather than Saul himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/26-19.htm
- Guzik: David knew the hatred came from Saul's own jealousy. He offered these other explanations to make it easier for Saul to repent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- "Go, serve other gods": Poole and JFB say this is what their actions meant. Driving David out of God's land and away from his worship exposed him to idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/26-19.htm
- Matthew Henry: what hurt most was not living among strangers but living among worshippers of strange gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/26-19.html
- Pett: in chapter 24 David has no thought of leaving Israel. Here he has clearly decided to go. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/1-samuel-26.html

**v. 20**
- Pulpit: David's main plea is not to be spared. It is not to be driven far from the land where God makes himself known, where an exile's life would sooner or later be cut short. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-26.html
- Matthew Henry: his blood would fall "before the face of the Lord," who will take note and avenge it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_026.cfm
- Clarke (quoted by Guzik) explains the partridge image. Arab hunters would flush partridges again and again until the birds were too tired to fly. Saul was hunting David the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/

**v. 21**
- Guzik: compared with chapter 24, Saul's words sound cold and mechanical. He seems regretful rather than repentant. Guzik quotes Meyer on worldly sorrow versus godly sorrow, and Morgan, who calls "I have played the fool" Saul's whole life story. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- Kelly: Saul confessed his sin, but there was "no conscience towards God." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/26-12.html
- Coffman thinks David saw at once that these were the words of a confirmed hypocrite. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-samuel-26.html?print=yes
- Constable lists Saul's earlier confessions in 15:30 and 24:17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-26.html
- Biblehub's summary is more positive: it calls the confession "a moment of repentance." https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/26.htm

**v. 22**
- Constable: David gave back the spear, the symbol of the right to rule. He may have kept the jug to remind Saul that he could still have taken his life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-26.html
- Ligonier: Saul would use that spear again against the Philistines, but never again against David. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-spares-saul-again

**vv. 23–24**
- Guzik ties this to Matthew 7:2 ("with the measure you use…"). David wanted a large measure of God's mercy, so he gave Saul a large measure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-26/
- Pulpit: David was willing to be judged by God's rule of rewarding each man's "righteousness and faithfulness." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-26.html
- Bible.org: David looks to the LORD to reward what he did that night. https://bible.org/seriespage/second-time-around-1-samuel-261-25

**v. 25**
- Pulpit: this blessing is much vaguer than 24:20–21, where Saul said plainly that David would be king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-samuel-26.html
- Matthew Henry: David could not trust Saul enough to go back with him, since someone who has broken his word once is hard to trust again. As far as the text shows, they never saw each other again. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_026.cfm
- Saul's remorse doesn't last, and in chapter 27 David has to flee to the Philistines. https://biblehub.com/1_samuel/26.htm

## Differences between Protestant traditions
I found none. The Reformed (Ligonier), Calvary Chapel (Guzik), Restoration Movement and Arminian (Coffman), and evangelical (Bible.org, Constable) writers I read all give the same basic reading: Saul is the LORD's anointed, vengeance belongs to God, and David must wait for God's timing.

## Other views
- **Are chapters 24 and 26 the same event told twice?**
  - Barnes thought it most likely that both accounts describe one event. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/26-1.html
  - Ellicott says Ewald and the Speaker's Commentary held this view, but Ellicott himself finds the two settings too different (a night raid on a camp versus a midday rest in a cave). https://studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/1-samuel-26.html
  - Coffman reports that Peake's Commentary and the International Critical Commentary call them two versions of one story. He rejects the idea and lists the differences. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-samuel-24.html
  - Hastings' Dictionary says scholars who see the books as compiled from several sources point to repeated stories of the same event as evidence. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/s/samuel-books-of.html
  - Deffinbaugh grants the similarities but takes them as deliberate: David gets a second chance after failing with Nabal in chapter 25. https://bible.org/seriespage/second-time-around-1-samuel-261-25
  - Constable quotes a writer who sees chapters 24–26 as one unit, with Nabal in the middle as a stand-in for Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/24-6.html
- **"Touch not my anointed" in popular teaching (vv. 9, 11, 23):** A Biblehub article cites David and Saul as the standard example. It warns that the phrase is sometimes used to dodge fair criticism or correction in churches, and says the text gives no one immunity from accountability. It does not name any particular movement. https://biblehub.com/q/what_does_'touch_not_my_anointed'_mean.htm
